reason: REFUTED on the citation, three ways, with a fourth objection to the cut itself. (1) THE NAMED EDITION IS NOT THE WITNESS. The source and the evidence both name The Works of Virgil, trans. John Dryden (Jacob Tonson, London, 1697), the folio first edition. The page actually read transcludes from Index:Virgil's Pastorals, Georgics and Aeneis - Dryden (1709) - volume 2.djvu, that is the Tonson octavo of 1709. I pulled the rendered page and read the Page namespace links myself. The capitals, the italics and above all the marginal line numbers that the locator depends on are the 1709 setting, not the 1697 folio, and the rules require the named edition to be the one whose wording is used. Nobody has opened a 1697 folio. (2) THE LINE NUMBERS DO NOT SURVIVE THEIR OWN PAGE. The 1709 margins on that page print 1170, 1175 and 1180. Counting forward from the 1170 marker (And soften into Flesh a Marble Face) gives To tame the Proud at 1176 and These are Imperial Arts at 1177. Counting backward from the 1180 marker (See great Marcellus! how, untir'd in Toils) gives the same, 1176 and 1177. Only the 1175 marker, sitting on To rule Mankind; and make the World obey, yields the verifier's 1177 and 1178, and that marker is the odd one out of three, almost certainly because the braced triplet (But, Rome, 'tis thine alone / To rule Mankind / Disposing Peace, and War, thy own Majestick Way) displaced it. Two of the three anchors on the very page cited contradict the locator. A line number that the page itself will not confirm is false precision. (3) THE LATIN LOCATOR IS WRONG. The source line says Latin 6.853 for the pair. Dryden reverses Virgil: To tame the Proud, the fetter'd Slave to free renders parcere subiectis et debellare superbos, which is 6.853, and These are Imperial Arts, and worthy thee renders hae tibi erunt artes, which is 6.852. The pair is 6.852 to 853, not 6.853, and the evidence block itself says 6.851 to 853, so the proposal contradicts its own witness inside one entry. (4) THE CUT MISREPRESENTS VIRGIL UNDER VIRGIL'S BYLINE, which is exactly the translation drift this track calls its main failure mode. parcere subiectis means spare the conquered; the fetter'd Slave to free is Dryden's invention and has no warrant in the Latin at all. The card prints Virgil as the byline, and a reader at six in the morning in a month about justice will read a line about freeing slaves that Virgil did not write. Worse, the two lines are the tail of a sentence whose head is To rule Mankind; and make the World obey, so These are Imperial Arts is a programme of empire, and the cut turns it into a liberation motto. The brief's own Virgil entry in the misattribution list warns about precisely this habit of lifting an Aeneid tag out of its speaker's situation. WHAT SURVIVES: the wording itself is genuine and I verified it character for character against the Wikisource text, capitals, the curly apostrophe in fetter'd and the semicolon after free all correct, verse slash correct, tag Poetry correct, Virgil at 1 for the year, not banned, not shipped, source line 98 characters with no dash. If the editor still wants it, ship the corrected source line below, put the 1709 Tonson octavo in the evidence as the edition read, and let the note say plainly that Dryden's fetter'd Slave to free is his own and not Virgil's parcere subiectis, and that Anchises is prescribing the arts of empire.
